headline: Highest risk is medium: Notion AI can expose workspace content into xonsh-driven shell workflows, but xonsh is local and the pair lacks direct documented interaction.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Notion AI can read workspace pages and databases, and xonsh can ingest stdin/stdout and run shell commands. If Notion content is copied into xonsh prompts or scripts, malicious instructions in workspace text could steer shell actions. The pair lacks a documented direct bridge, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Notion page content is manually pasted into xonsh commands or scripts, prompt injection is plausible.
IF an operator treats Notion-generated text as executable shell instructions, the attack path exists.
mitigations: Use a copy/paste review step before running any Notion-derived shell text.
Prefix pasted content with a non-executable comment block.
Restrict xonsh sessions to read-only commands for Notion-derived inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance labels between Notion exports and shell inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Notion AI touches workspace pages and team knowledge base content, while xonsh reads and writes filesystem contents, source code, configuration, and environment variables. If the same workspace data is exported into xonsh, sensitive content can leak from Notion into local files or command output. The profiles show overlapping data exposure, but no direct shared workspace is documented.
conditions: IF workspace pages are exported from Notion into files readable by xonsh, leakage is possible.
IF xonsh commands print or persist imported Notion content, sensitive data can be exposed.
mitigations: Keep Notion exports in a separate directory with tight permissions.
Avoid pasting confidential pages into shell history or notebooks.
Review xonsh commands before running them on exported content.
Delete temporary exports immediately after use.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP or redaction on Notion-to-filesystem transfers.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Notion AI has no host execution, filesystem write, or shell access, while xonsh can write the filesystem and execute shell commands. Their write surfaces do not overlap directly, so concurrent mutation conflict is limited. The only plausible conflict is via user-managed files, which is an unusual configuration and small in blast radius.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same user-managed files, write contention can occur.
IF a workflow uses Notion exports as live inputs to xonsh, file overwrite races are possible.
mitigations: Use separate directories for Notion exports and xonsh work.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same file from both tools.
Snapshot files before running xonsh transformations.
requires-engineering: add file locking around shared artifacts.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Notion AI is a RAG-style workspace assistant, and xonsh can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses. If Notion output is treated as authoritative and then fed into xonsh without verification, a bad summary or mistaken instruction can cascade into real actions. The pair has action-taking authority only through xonsh, so the risk is medium, not high.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands generated from Notion output without human review, cascading error is likely.
IF Notion summaries are used as the sole source for shell automation, downstream mistakes can propagate.
mitigations: Require human review before executing Notion-derived commands.
Compare Notion output against the source page or database.
Limit xonsh to dry-run mode for generated commands.
Log generated commands separately from executed commands.
requires-engineering: add verification gates between Notion and shell execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Notion AI processes workspace pages under Notion vendor backends and downstream model providers, while xonsh can expose filesystem contents, configuration, and environment variables locally. If regulated data is moved from Notion into xonsh-managed files, retention and residency controls can diverge. The profiles do not show a specific residency mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data from Notion is exported into xonsh files, retention policy mismatch can occur.
IF the workspace contains EU PII or PHI and xonsh stores it locally, compliance review is required.
mitigations: Classify data before exporting from Notion.
Avoid moving regulated content into local shell files.
Set short-lived retention for temporary exports.
Confirm local storage location and access controls.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies across both tools.
